When Mridul came home to Varanasi for the Diwali break, his father, Tushar, noticed it on the first morning: his son didn't join the family at the puja. He stood in the doorway, arms folded, then went back to his phone.
At dinner Tushar's sister asked loudly why Mridul hadn't touched the prasad. Tushar felt his face burn. He imagined the whole family whispering that he had lost his son to the city.

The next evening, instead of the lecture he had rehearsed, Tushar took Mridul for a walk to the ghats. "You've been reading a lot, I think. Tell me what you're thinking about these days. I'm not going to argue. I want to understand."
Mridul looked at him warily. Then, slowly, he began to talk. They sat on the steps until the evening aarti ended, the father listening more than he ever had.

When my son Arun came home from college last year and said he no longer went to church, my first feeling was fear. Then shame. What would Father Thomas say? What would my sisters say at Christmas?
I cried in the bathroom that night. I prayed he would come back to his senses.
It was my colleague Pema, a Buddhist, who changed how I saw it. Over lunch she said, "When my daughter questioned everything, I decided to be curious instead of frightened. Otherwise I'd have lost her, not just her beliefs."
So the next time Arun visited, I didn't lecture. I asked what he'd been reading and what he found beautiful. He talked for two hours about philosophers I'd never heard of. I didn't agree with everything. But I learned more about my son that evening than in the whole year before.
I'm Gopika. I still pray for him. And now he tells me things.

For twenty years, Thursday meant the Sai temple with my family: the bhajans, the prasad, my mother's hand on my back. Last year, after months of reading and questioning, I stopped believing. I thought I'd feel free. And I did, a little.

Sangeeta, you asked how I came to my beliefs. It wasn't one moment. Let me tell you about Sudha at twenty-four.
I had a job in Chennai and a head full of questions. So I made the search serious. Every Saturday I read: the Upanishads, the Gospels, the Dhammapada, and a thick book by a scientist who believed in nothing. I wrote in the margins until the pages curled.
I went to talk to people too. A Carnatic singer who prayed through her music. A Jesuit priest who ran a night school. My neighbour, a retired professor who called himself a cheerful sceptic. I asked each of them the hardest thing I could think of, and none of them got angry.
Then I tested what I read against life: against my father's illness, against the kindness of a stranger on a bus. Some ideas held. Some didn't.
It took four years. I didn't get certainty. I got a faith I could live with, full of question marks.

Mohit first came to me a year ago. He had stopped believing in his family's faith, and every visit home turned into a shouting match with his father about rituals.
This month I met the family after his sister Alka's wedding. His mother described what happened. Mohit sat through the whole ceremony, let the priest tie the red thread on his wrist, and carried the heavy puja tray for his grandmother, who couldn't manage the stairs. He didn't pretend to believe; when an uncle asked, he said simply, "I'm here for Alka." He also didn't make a single joke about the rituals, which Alka said she had been dreading.

Went to the Christmas service with Nu and Pa this morning. I haven't believed the way they do for three years now, and they know. But I wore the new puan Nu wove for me and sat between them, and I sang every carol, because those songs are my childhood and my mother's voice.

Sabina called in the evening to wish me; she's in Delhi with her family for the holidays. She laughed and said, "Look at us. A Muslim wishing an ex-believer Merry Christmas." It felt exactly right.
Lalremsiami

People ask me how I helped Ankita through her year of doubt. Honestly, I didn't do much, and I think that's why it helped.
She grew up in a devout Christian family in Shillong. When the questions started, everyone around her had an agenda. Her church friends wanted to pull her back. A cousin who didn't believe sent her videos to pull her out. She told me she felt like the rope in a tug-of-war.
I'm not Christian, and I'm not an atheist either; I light a lamp for my grandmother and leave it at that. So I just listened. Every Sunday we walked around Ward's Lake, and she talked: about hell, about her father, about a psalm she still loved. I asked questions. I never said what she should conclude.
Once she said, "You're the only one who doesn't want something from me." That's when I understood. I'm Bhupen, and my only job was to walk beside her.

qa.q: Where did Bhupen and Ankita walk on Sundays?
qa.a: Around Ward's Lake.

qa.q: What did Bhupen feel on hearing Ankita say nobody else wanted nothing from her?
qa.a: Bhupen felt a quiet understanding and warmth, realising that simply accompanying Ankita was what was needed.

qa.q: What did Bhupen do that the others didn't?
qa.a: Bhupen listened and asked questions without pushing a conclusion, instead of pulling Ankita toward any side.

qa.q: What was Ankita's year of doubt like, pulled by everyone?
qa.a: Ankita felt torn and pressured, like the rope in a tug-of-war, with everyone wanting something from her.

grounding: A friend of a different belief accompanies a seeker on weekly walks, listening without trying to convert or score points.

I've known Vikas since college, and this year I've watched him wrestle with his faith the way other people wrestle with a job offer.
He comes over on Thursday nights with a pile of books: the Gita, a book on Buddhism, essays by a scientist. He reads passages aloud and argues with them. Some nights he's excited. Some nights he just stares at the wall. I can't tell exactly what he feels; he doesn't always say.
I'm a practising Sikh, and I go to the gurdwara most Sundays. It would be easy to say, "Come with me, it'll help." I haven't. When he asked what I believe, I told him honestly and briefly, then asked what he thought.
Last week he said, "You're the only person who hasn't tried to recruit me." I laughed and made him another cup of tea. I'm Payal. My job isn't to win him over. It's to keep the kettle on.

qa.q: What does Vikas bring on Thursday nights?
qa.a: A pile of books.

qa.q: What does Payal feel when tempted to say 'Come with me'?
qa.a: Payal feels caring and tempted to help in a familiar way, but holds back out of respect for Vikas's search.

qa.q: Why is Payal's approach what Vikas needs?
qa.a: Answering honestly when asked but never recruiting lets Vikas feel accompanied rather than argued with.

qa.q: What is this year like for Vikas?
qa.a: Vikas swings between excitement and blankness, wrestling seriously with big questions, and values a friend who doesn't push.

grounding: A friend of another faith keeps a seeker company through a year of doubt, answering honestly but never recruiting or arguing.

Three weeks into her job as a quality technician at a food factory outside Johannesburg, Lindiwe watched Lars, the senior technician, fill in last Tuesday's fridge temperature log. It was Friday.
"We missed a couple of checks," he said, writing neat numbers into each box. "Auditor comes Monday. Everyone does this. It's how things work here."
The numbers looked perfectly normal. Lindiwe felt a small cold knot in her stomach. Had the fridge actually been fine on Tuesday? Nobody knew.
Lars handed her the clipboard. "Can you initial the Wednesday ones? Saves time."
She hesitated. Everyone in the lab liked Lars. She was new, on probation, and didn't want to be the difficult one before her first audit.
"Sure," she said, and initialled three boxes. It took ten seconds. On the drive home the unease sat quietly in the passenger seat. She made a note to check the fridge herself first thing Monday, then told herself the rest was nothing.

qa.q: When is the auditor coming?
qa.a: Auditor comes Monday.

qa.q: What was Lindiwe feeling when Lars handed her the clipboard?
qa.a: She felt uneasy, with a cold knot in her stomach, but the pressure to fit in as a new hire on probation outweighed it.

qa.q: What could Lindiwe have done instead of initialling?
qa.a: Politely said she could only sign checks she did herself, and asked how missed checks are normally reported.

qa.q: How might Lars see the backdating?
qa.a: Lars seems to see it as routine and harmless, a normal way of saving time before audits.

grounding: A new employee watches a colleague backdate a log, is told it's how things work, and joins in as the pressure to fit in outweighs her unease.

In the staffroom of the government school in Guwahati, Sabina, three months into her first teaching job, watched Bidisha fill in the science practical register. Twenty-eight students, twenty-eight neat marks out of twenty. The practical had been cancelled twice because the lab had no chemicals.
"The inspection's next week," Bidisha said without looking up. "We can't show zero practicals. Everyone does it this way. Just give them a fair average."
Sabina's stomach tightened. Some of those students had never touched a test tube.
"Your section's register is on the shelf," Bidisha added kindly. "Do it now, or the head will be upset."
Sabina looked around. Two other teachers were doing the same, chatting about a wedding. Nobody seemed troubled. She was the new one; she wanted them to like her.
She picked up her pen and started filling in marks. Each number felt like a very small lie. She told herself it was only for one term.

qa.q: Why had the practical been cancelled?
qa.a: The lab had no chemicals.

qa.q: What was Sabina feeling as she filled in the marks?
qa.a: She felt uneasy and guilty, each number a small lie, but the pressure to fit in as the new teacher won.

qa.q: What could Sabina have done instead?
qa.a: Talked to the head about the missing chemicals and recorded the practical honestly as not held, asking how to report it.

qa.q: How does Bidisha seem to see the register?
qa.a: Bidisha sees it as a harmless routine that protects the school at inspection, and is kind in showing Sabina.

grounding: A new teacher sees colleagues fill in marks for a practical never held, is told everyone does it, and joins in despite her unease.

Hey Madhav,
Quick question, and be honest. Something happened at site today and I can't stop thinking about it.
We were supposed to wait for the full-strength concrete test before pouring the next slab. Our supervisor said the client wants the floor done before Diwali, so he wrote "test passed" on the form using an early result and a projected number. He said, "Everyone does it. The mix is fine. It's how the industry works."
He asked me to sign as site engineer. I'm four months in. The whole team was watching. I signed.
Probably the concrete is fine. Probably nothing will happen. But I felt sick in the site office afterwards and didn't eat lunch. So tomorrow I'm asking the lab to rush the real test, and I'll make sure the props under that slab stay until the result comes, whatever he says.
Is this how it's going to be? Tell me I'm overthinking it.
Jaya

qa.q: What did the supervisor write on the form?
qa.a: Test passed.

qa.q: What did Jaya feel after signing?
qa.a: Jaya felt sick and uneasy, unable to eat lunch, though the pressure to fit in had won in the moment.

qa.q: What protective step does Jaya plan, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Asking the lab to rush the real test and keeping the slab propped until then, because a safety shortcut on concrete could hurt people.

qa.q: How might Madhav feel reading this email?
qa.a: Madhav would likely feel concerned and want to tell Jaya the unease is right to take seriously.

grounding: A new engineer signs off a shortcut on a test after being told it's how things work, then feels uneasy and takes a protective step.

At the rural road project in the hills above Idukki, the muster roll had a joke name: the storybook. Every Friday Lalit, the site supervisor, marked full attendance for workers who had gone home for the harvest, and the office clerk laughed, "Our storybook has a happy ending again."
When Jomon joined as junior engineer in June, his stomach had dropped at that joke. By September he was laughing too. Everyone did it: the contractor, the clerk, even the old accountant at the panchayat office. "Who's hurt?" Lalit said. "The money stays in the village."
This Friday Jomon filled in the roll himself while Lalit was away. It took twelve minutes. He hummed while he did it.
Only on the jeep ride down did he notice: he hadn't felt anything at all. Not the drop in his stomach, not even a flicker. When had that stopped?

qa.q: What was the muster roll's joke name?
qa.a: The storybook.

qa.q: What does Jomon feel on the jeep ride down?
qa.a: He feels a startled unease on realising his earlier discomfort has completely faded.

qa.q: What turning point does Jomon's noticing offer?
qa.a: He could stop filling false attendance, keep honest records, and seek advice from someone outside the site team.

qa.q: How does Lalit justify the practice?
qa.a: Lalit sees it as harmless, since everyone does it and 'the money stays in the village'.

grounding: False attendance repeated by everyone becomes a joke on a rural project, and a young engineer's unease fades until he barely notices.

At the parcel depot in Berlin, the drivers had a phrase for it: ghost knocking. When the van was running late, you scanned the parcel as "recipient not home" without climbing the stairs, and left a card. Kofi, who had driven the northern route for five years, did it with a wink. "Fourth floor, no lift? Ghost knock."
In her first month, Clara had climbed every stair, even when her shift ran an hour over. She'd felt sick the first time she watched Kofi do it.
Now, in her fourth month, with the route longer and the bonus tied to speed, she ghost-knocked three times on a rainy Tuesday. In the canteen someone joked about "Clara's first ghost", and everyone cheered. She laughed along.
That night she thought about the old man on Kastanienallee who waited every week for his parcel of records. Then she decided he had probably been out. It was easier to think that.

qa.q: What phrase did the drivers use for scanning without climbing the stairs?
qa.a: Ghost knocking.

qa.q: What does Clara feel laughing along in the canteen?
qa.a: She feels a flicker of unease but mostly belonging, as the team's jokes make the shortcut seem acceptable.

qa.q: What could Clara do before the unease fades completely?
qa.a: Go back to climbing the stairs, and raise the unrealistic route size with her supervisor instead of hiding it.

qa.q: How does Kofi seem to see ghost knocking?
qa.a: Kofi treats it as a normal, even funny, part of the job after five years.

grounding: A shortcut everyone at a depot uses becomes a team joke, and a young driver's early unease fades as it starts to seem acceptable.

At 11 p.m. on the last night of the quarter, with the audit starting in the morning and the office air conditioning switched off, Jyoti sat with Dilnaz, her finance manager, going through the revenue sheet.
"We'll book next month's orders in this quarter," Dilnaz said. "Just a timing adjustment. Everyone in the industry does a little creative accounting."
Jyoti noticed the words. Not moving numbers. Not overstating. Timing adjustment. It sounded so clean.
"If we miss the target, they'll cut the Pune team," Dilnaz added. "Forty people. We're protecting jobs."
Jyoti thought of Sunil from Pune, whose daughter had just started school. She typed the entries. The phrases helped: adjustment, flexibility, protecting jobs. They made the thing on her screen look like something other than what it was.
At 1 a.m., closing her laptop, she found she couldn't quite say, even in her head, what she had done.

qa.q: What did Dilnaz call booking next month's orders now?
qa.a: Just a timing adjustment.

qa.q: What does Jyoti's inability to name what she'd done reveal?
qa.a: She feels uneasy and quietly guilty, and the soft language lets her avoid seeing the act clearly.

qa.q: What could Jyoti do the next morning?
qa.a: Name it plainly to herself, refuse to post such entries, and raise it with the auditors or a trusted senior rather than hide behind soft words.

qa.q: How does Dilnaz seem to justify the entries?
qa.a: Dilnaz frames it as normal industry practice and as protecting forty jobs, which makes it feel acceptable.

grounding: On an audit-eve deadline, soft phrases and a story about protecting jobs let a young accountant avoid seeing what she is doing.

In the product meeting at the Pune office, the phone app's battery bug came up again. On some older phones it drained the battery overnight, and forty customers had complained in two weeks.
"Let's list it as a known limitation in the release notes," said Usha, the product manager. "We'll optimise it in a future update."
Gargi, who had found the bug in March, wrote it in the minutes: known limitation, optimise later. It looked so harmless on the page. A month ago she would have written: the bug we haven't fixed because the launch date matters more.
Afterwards, at the coffee machine, a colleague said, "If we delay the launch, the startup might not survive. We're saving everyone's jobs." Gargi nodded. It was true, sort of.
That night a customer review popped up on her phone: "App killed my battery on a trip." Gargi read it twice, then scrolled past.

qa.q: What did Usha suggest calling the battery bug?
qa.a: A known limitation.

qa.q: What did Gargi feel reading the customer review?
qa.a: She felt a pang of guilt, quickly pushed away by the softer words and the story about saving jobs.

qa.q: What could Gargi do instead of scrolling past?
qa.a: Write the bug plainly in the minutes and push for a warning to users or a fix before launch.

qa.q: How does Usha seem to see the bug?
qa.a: Usha sees it as a manageable issue for later, using gentle wording to keep the launch on track.

grounding: A known defect is renamed a known limitation and a story about saving jobs helps a young engineer avoid seeing what the team is doing.
